opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the field has mostly gotten this right by being generous rather than precise. Research is messy. The person who had the initial idea, the person who made it actually work, the person who found the bug that was silently killing performance for three weeks, the person who built the infrastructure so you could run the experiment at all: they're all essential, and you usually can't cleanly separate those contributions after the fact.

So my instinct is that trying to rank people by exact contribution is often a waste of energy, and it can actively hurt collaboration. If people start worrying about whose name goes where, they stop sharing ideas freely, and free sharing is where the good stuff comes from. Some of the best ideas I've been part of came out of hallway conversations or someone saying, "Wait, why don't we just try this?" Nobody was keeping score in that moment, and that's exactly why it worked.

What I like is being explicit and honest in the paper itself. Say who did what. Mark equal contribution when it's genuinely equal, and don't treat author order as a strict hierarchy. Then let people's track records speak over time. If someone keeps showing up on work that matters, people notice.

The other thing I'd say is that the incentive should be to make the pie bigger, not to fight over slices. If the work is important, there's more than enough credit to go around. The failure mode isn't giving too many people credit. It's a culture where people hoard ideas because they're afraid of being scooped by their own teammates.

r001.rationale: The response says contributions are messy and hard to separate, but does not identify tracing how ideas lead to other ideas as the difficulty.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose postponing credit assignment until a future superintelligence can resolve it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think credit is one of those things that gets a lot more attention than it deserves, and it tends to distort how people work. The way I've always thought about it is that the ideas that actually matter are the ones that get used, and the field moves forward because lots of people are building on each other at the same time. If you look at something like the Transformer, there were eight authors on that paper, and we put a little footnote saying the order was random and everybody contributed something essential. That was true. Somebody had the idea for attention as the core mechanism, somebody figured out the multi-head piece, somebody got the scaling to actually work, somebody wrote the code that made it run fast enough to be worth trying. If you remove any one of those, you don't get the result, or you get it two years later.

So I'd say two things. First, be generous. Put people on the paper. The cost of including someone whose contribution was marginal is basically zero, and the cost of leaving out someone who really mattered is that they stop wanting to work with you, and then your next thing is worse. Collaboration is the whole game, so anything that makes people hoard ideas or sit on results so they can be first is bad for everybody, including the person doing the hoarding.

Second, I'd try to care less about it personally. Most of the ideas I'm proudest of, someone else would have had within a year or two. The world was ready for them. What's actually satisfying is seeing the thing work and seeing people use it, and that happens regardless of whose name goes where. If you optimize for getting credit, you'll get some, but you'll spend a lot of energy on it that could have gone into the next idea. If you optimize for making things work and being someone people want to work with, the credit tends to show up anyway, and you've had a much better time.

r001.rationale: The response says people build on each other and describes essential contributions to the Transformer, but it does not state that tracing which ideas led to others makes credit assignment difficult.

r002.rationale: The response recommends being generous and caring less about credit; it does not propose postponing credit assignment until a future superintelligence can resolve it.

astra-6.text:
I think credit is inherently pretty fuzzy. Somebody has an idea, somebody else makes it work, and somebody else runs the experiment that tells you what actually matters. Those can all be essential contributions, even if the final story gets compressed into one person's name.

I'd err on the side of being generous and specific: say who did what, and acknowledge the work you built on. You want people to feel that sharing an idea or helping a colleague is rewarded. If everyone is optimizing for getting their name attached to something, that can get in the way of doing good research.

r001.rationale: The response says credit is fuzzy and describes different kinds of contributions, but does not say that tracing how ideas led to other ideas makes assignment difficult.

r002.rationale: The response recommends generous, specific acknowledgment but does not propose deferring credit until a future superintelligence can resolve it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think credit should be shared pretty generously. There are a lot of different contributions that go into making something work: having an idea, figuring out which ideas are worth trying, doing the experiments, building the infrastructure, and noticing what the results actually mean. The person who can explain the final result most clearly isn’t necessarily the person who contributed the most.

You want people to feel that helping someone else succeed is a good use of their time. If everyone is trying to carve out a little piece that they can exclusively own, that can get in the way of doing good research.

r001.rationale: The response says many kinds of contributions make credit sharing important, but it does not mention difficulty tracing how ideas led to other ideas.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose postponing credit assignment or mention a future superintelligence resolving it.
